Orkney: Where History and Horizon Meet

Orkney sits just off Scotland's north coast, separated from the mainland by the Pentland Firth — one of the most treacherous stretches of water in Britain. Despite their northern location, the islands have a gentle character: rolling farmland, ancient monuments older than the pyramids, and a remarkably mild climate thanks to the Gulf Stream. For motorcyclists, Orkney offers a unique blend of history, scenery, and island riding.

Getting There

Two ferry operators serve Orkney:

  • NorthLink Ferries — Aberdeen to Kirkwall (6 hours) or Scrabster to Stromness (90 minutes)
  • Pentland Ferries — Gills Bay to St Margaret's Hope (1 hour), the quickest crossing

The Scrabster-Stromness and Gills Bay-St Margaret's Hope routes work best for motorcyclists on the NC500 who want to add Orkney as an extension.

The Mainland

Orkney's Mainland is the largest island and contains most of the major attractions. The Heart of Neolithic Orkney is a UNESCO World Heritage Site comprising Skara Brae (a 5,000-year-old village), the Ring of Brodgar (a stone circle), Maeshowe (a chambered cairn), and the Standing Stones of Stenness.

Riding Orkney

Orkney's roads are well-maintained and mostly flat. The A960 and A964 form a circuit of the Mainland that covers the main attractions in about 80 miles. Traffic is light and the roads flow gently through farmland with frequent sea views. The Churchill Barriers — causeways built during WWII to protect the naval base at Scapa Flow — connect the Mainland to South Ronaldsay and are a unique riding experience.

Orkney's appeal is subtle rather than dramatic. The light is extraordinary, the history is humbling, and the islands grow on you quietly until you don't want to leave.

Scapa Flow and WWII History

Scapa Flow is a vast natural harbour that served as the Royal Navy's main base in both World Wars. The German High Seas Fleet was scuttled here in 1919 — some wrecks are still visible at low tide. The Italian Chapel on Lamb Holm, built by POWs from two Nissen huts, is one of Orkney's most moving sites.

Outer Islands

Inter-island ferries connect the Mainland to smaller islands. Hoy has dramatic clifftop scenery including the Old Man of Hoy sea stack. Rousay is called the Egypt of the North for its concentration of archaeological sites. Taking your motorcycle on the inter-island ferries is straightforward and inexpensive.

Practical Information

Fuel and facilities are available in Kirkwall and Stromness. Accommodation ranges from hotels to B&Bs and campsites. The weather is windy — expect constant wind and dress accordingly. Orkney is milder than you'd expect, but rain is frequent. Allow 2-3 days for the Mainland and a further day for each outer island you visit.

faq.q: Which ferry should I take to Orkney?
faq.a: Two operators serve the islands. NorthLink runs Scrabster to Stromness in 90 minutes and Aberdeen to Kirkwall in six hours, while Pentland Ferries runs the quickest crossing from Gills Bay to St Margaret's Hope in one hour. The Scrabster and Gills Bay routes work best for NC500 riders adding Orkney as an extension.

faq.q: What are the must-see sites on Orkney?
faq.a: The Heart of Neolithic Orkney is a UNESCO World Heritage Site comprising Skara Brae, a 5,000-year-old village, the Ring of Brodgar stone circle, Maeshowe chambered cairn and the Standing Stones of Stenness. Scapa Flow and the moving Italian Chapel on Lamb Holm, built by wartime POWs, are also essential stops.

faq.q: What is the riding like on Orkney?
faq.a: Orkney's roads are well-maintained and mostly flat. The A960 and A964 form a circuit of the Mainland covering the main attractions in about 80 miles, with light traffic and frequent sea views. The Churchill Barriers, wartime causeways connecting the Mainland to South Ronaldsay, offer a unique riding experience.

faq.q: How long should I spend on Orkney?
faq.a: Allow two to three days for the Mainland and a further day for each outer island you visit. Inter-island ferries connect to smaller islands such as Hoy, with its Old Man of Hoy sea stack, and Rousay, the Egypt of the North. Taking your motorcycle on these ferries is straightforward and inexpensive.

Orkney is windy year-round, so dress accordingly and expect constant wind. Thanks to the Gulf Stream the islands are milder than you would expect for their latitude, but rain is frequent. The quality of light is extraordinary, particularly in the long summer days.
